content: In chemistry, a mixture is defined as a substance formed by the physical combination of two or more distinct materials, without any chemical reaction taking place. The individual components in a mixture do not chemically bond with one another. Typically, mixtures can be separated back into their original components through physical means. Examples of mixtures include fruit salad, ocean water, and soil. Specific examples of heterogeneous mixtures include salt water, iron filings, sulfur, and salt mixed with sand. Mixtures are created through mechanical blending or mixing of chemical substances, such as elements and compounds, without the formation of chemical bonds or any chemical transformation. As a result, each component in the mixture retains its original chemical properties and composition. Although no chemical changes occur in a mixture, its physical properties, such as melting point, may differ from those of its individual components. Mixtures can generally be separated using mechanical methods. They are classified as either homogeneous or heterogeneous. Homogeneous Mixtures Homogeneous mixtures are characterized by uniform and consistent properties throughout. The particles in these mixtures are evenly distributed, ensuring that any given portion of the mixture has the same composition and properties. Examples of homogeneous mixtures include solutions and certain alloys (though not all alloys are homogeneous). A homogeneous mixture consists of only one phase, such as gasoline or margarine. Solutions A solution is a type of homogeneous mixture in which one or more substances (the solutes) are dissolved in another substance (the solvent). In solutions, the particles are extremely small, typically within the size range of atoms, small molecules, or small ions, measuring less than 1 nanometer (nm) in all dimensions. Examples include salt or sugar dissolved in water, or gold dissolved in mercury. Liquids can dissolve into one another, and in some cases, liquids can dissolve into gases, such as water vapor in the atmosphere. Common examples of solutions include carbonated beverages, where carbon dioxide is dissolved in the liquid through carbonation. Solutions exhibit properties known as colligative properties, which change depending on the concentration of the solute. Solubility is a key property of compounds in solutions. Colloidal Dispersions Colloids are another type of homogeneous mixture in which the particles of one or more components have at least one dimension within the range of 1 to 1000 nanometers, making them larger than those in a solution but smaller than those in a suspension. A colloid, or colloidal dispersion, typically consists of components in one or two phases. Colloids exhibit the Tyndall effect, where light is scattered as it passes through the mixture. Unlike suspensions, colloids do not settle over time. Examples of colloidal dispersions include jelly, milk, blood, paint, fog, and glue. Heterogeneous Mixtures Heterogeneous mixtures are those with inconsistent and non-uniform composition. The individual components of a heterogeneous mixture can be mechanically separated from one another. Examples of heterogeneous mixtures include salad, trail mix, and granite. Suspensions A suspension is a type of heterogeneous mixture in which the particles of at least one component are larger than 1 micrometer (1000 nanometers) in at least one dimension, making them larger than colloidal particles. Unlike colloids, suspensions will eventually settle over time. An example of a suspension is sand in water. The particles in suspensions are large enough to scatter light, a phenomenon known as the Tyndall effect.
